title: AE against North Lanarkshire Council
text:
2026UT48 
Ref: UTS/AP/25/0150 
 
DECISION OF 
 
 
Lady Carmichael 
 
 
ON AN APPEAL 
IN THE CASE OF 
 
 
AE 
per Cairn Legal Limited 
 
Appellant 
 
- and - 
 
 
North Lanarkshire Council 
Per Anderson Strathern 
 
Respondent 
 
FTS Case Reference: FTS/HEC/AC/25/0026 
 
 
Appellant: Mr Iain Nisbet, solicitor; Cairn Legal Limited 
Respondent: Mr David Anderson, advocate; Anderson Strathern 
 
1 May 2026 
 
Decision 
 
The Upper Tribunal for Scotland refuses the appeal. 
 
Reasons 
 
1. The appellant made a claim under the Equality Act 2010 (the 2010 Act) to the First -tier 
Tribunal for Scotland (FTS) that the respondent local authority discriminated against her

son (the child) in relation to his education. She submitted also that the respondent had 
breached Article 28 of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC), 
founding on the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child (Incorp oration) 
(Scotland) Act 2024 (the 2024 Act). 
 
2. The relevant procedural rules are contained in the First- tier Tribunal for Scotland Health 
and Education Chamber Rules of Procedure 2018 (the 2018 rules). 
 
3. The appellant’s argument is that the FTS made a decision to reject her claim after hearing 
from only one witness. Essentially her complaint is one of a procedural error that has 
resulted in unfairness to her. 
 
Background 
 
4. There was no dispute that the child had a disability as defined in the 2010 Act. 
 
5. From August 2024 the child attended a particular facility (the SA), which is managed by the 
respondent, and is part of the campus of a mainstream high school. The FTS found that 
the purpose of the provision was to support the child to return to mainstream education. 
Provision of that sort was normally delivered in a single eight-week block, which might be 
extended. The education was delivered as part of t he respondent’s outreach provision. 
The child in fact received education there for two eight -week blocks, with a further 
extension of two weeks. On 13 January 2025 witness A wrote to the appellant and told 
her that the child’s education at the facility would be coming to an end. 
 
6. The appellant’s claim was that the removal of the child from the facility at the SA in January 
2025 constituted unlawful discrimination. The remedy she sought was reinstatement to 
the SA. As well as asking for that remedy, in response to the question, “what result are 
you seeking”, the appellant wrote: 
 
“ Also for the Education department to see and understand what impact this has on [the 
child].” 
 
7. In her claim form she also referred to Article 28 of the UNCRC. The reference in the claim 
form is simply a reference to section 6 of the 2024 Act, and quotation of the terms of Article 
28 of the UNCRC. A statement of “reasons and grounds” produced for the FTS by the

appellant narrated that she believed that the respond ent had breached Article 28. The 
statement goes on to summarise the terms of Article 28. 
 
8. The FTS found that between January and May 2025, the child was introduced to staff in the 
respondent’s ‘cluster team’, in order that he could continue to receive 1:1 tuition. The 
cluster team provided support once a child had settled following outreach sup port. The 
child’s education at the SA with the outreach team had gone well. He received education 
in maths, English and history, at National 4 level. One of the aims of the movement of the 
child’s support to the cluster team would have been to increase the number of subjects the 
child would be taught, from the three taught within the outreach provision. 
 
9. The FTS found also that outreach provision at the SA building was to end for all pupils 
from about 8 September 2025, because the respondent had decided to change the use of the 
building. It would no longer be used for outreach provision, but for pupils with the most 
significant social, emotional and behavioural difficulties in the respondent’s area. It found 
that that once the new pupil group began to attend the SA, it was unlikely to be a peaceful, 
quiet, learning space. 
 
The procedure followed by the FTS at the hearing 
 
10. The FTS heard evidence from witness A on 27 August 2025. It then adjourned. The 
tribunal directed the respondent to prepare and intimate a document setting out its 
proposed plan for the child’s “immediate future education”. It gave reasons for taking 
that course. 
 
11. A’s witness statement had disclosed that the change in use of the SA, with the new group 
of pupils attending, would be likely to happen in August 2025. In his oral evidence he said 
that the date on which the outreach service would cease to operate at the SA was 8 
September 2025. It was in the light of that information that the FTS allowed the appellant 
time to consider whether she wished to reformulate the remedy she sought. In giving 
reasons for the decision to adjourn and give directions the tribunal noted that it seemed 
very unlikely from the witness statements before it that witness A’s evidence about the 
cessation of the outreach service would be contradicted. 
 
12. When the hearing recommenced for a second day, following a period of adjournment, the 
appellant made it clear that she did not wish to amend the remedy she was seeking. The

FTS decided that it did not need to hear any further evidence in relation to the claim, 
because it was clear from the statements of the witnesses other than A and the appellant 
that their evidence would not have added anything to the question of the appropriateness 
of the remedy being sought. 
 
13. The FTS did not decide whether the treatment of the child constituted discrimination, 
because it considered that it would not be appropriate to grant the remedy sought by the 
appellant, given the information it had from the witness about the future of the facility. 
 
14. When it was considering the appropriateness of the remedy that the appellant was seeking, 
the FTS expressed the view that a finding of discrimination was not a remedy, and that it 
did not have power to grant a declaratory remedy. It took the view that a declarator would 
not be an “order” of the sort contemplated in paragraph 9(1) of Schedule 17 to the 2010 Act. 
It contrasted that provision with section 124(2) of the 2010 Act, which gives an Employment 
Tribunal the power to make a declaration as to the rights of a complainant and respondent. 
 
The appellant’s arguments 
 
15. The appellant submitted, first, that the tribunal should have determined whether unlawful 
discrimination had occurred. If it had, it was then empowered to make such orders as it 
thought fit: Schedule 17, paragraph 9(3). It was not restricted to making an order of a type 
specifically identified by the appellant. It should also have determined whether the 
respondent had breached the UNCRC requirements as defined in the 2024 Act. If the 
respondent had done so, the FTS would have had the power to grant a remedy under 
section 8 of that Act. 
 
16. Second, the FTS should not have reached a conclusion on remedies before hearing from all 
of the witnesses. The appellant had been prepared to lead three witnesses, who might 
have given relevant evidence. Parties were entitled to call witnesses: rules 79(6) and 85 of 
the 2018 rules. The witnesses had no opportunity to address the issue of the 
appropriateness of the remedy that the appellant was seeking. 
 
17. In oral argument Mr Nisbet submitted that it would have been appropriate for the tribunal 
to conclude that the respondent had failed in its duty to make reasonable adjustments by 
reference to section 20(3) of the 2010 Act, and grant a declaratory remedy re flecting that 
conclusion. The provision, criterion or practice that had placed the child at a disadvantage

was the rule that placement at the SA was on a short term basis only. Two of the appellant’s 
witnesses, Ms S and Ms C, could have informed the tribunal in relation to “transition 
planning” and failures to make reasonable adjustments. 
 
18. Third, the FTS had erred in concluding that it did not have power to grant a declaratory 
remedy. Parliament had intended the tribunal to have a wide range of remedies available 
to it: AA and CC v Secretary of State for Education and others [2022] EWHC 1613 (Admin), at 
paragraphs 108-114, citing statements made by Baroness Blackstone in the House of Lords 
during the passage of the Special Educational Needs and Disability Act 2001.There was 
authority in relation to earlier legislation that it was competent to grant a declarator that a 
respondent had discriminated unlawfully, at least as a precursor to other remedies, and 
when the pleadings provided sufficient specification as to the nature of the discrimination: 
S v K School 2009 SLT (Sh Ct) 86, paragraph 40. It was to be expected that a public authority 
would alter its practices in the light of a finding of unlawfulness: East Lothian Council v SH 
2026 UT 14, paragraph 42. 
 
19. AA was an unsuccessful challenge to the statutory exclusion of damages as a remedy, by 
reference to Article 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights (the ECHR) read with 
Article 1 or 2 of Protocol 1 (A1P1 or A2P1) or Article 8. The court was satisfied that the issue 
fell with in the ambit of A1P1 but not that there was a difference in treatment for the 
purposes of Article 14. The court nonetheless went on to consider the issue of justification, 
and it was in this context that it e xamined the statements of Baroness Blackstone in the 
House of Lords. Saini J found that if there were any difference of treatment for the purposes 
of Article 14, the state had established that it was justified. One of the matters that he took 
into account was the range of remedies, other than financial compensation, that the tribunal 
could award: paragraphs 120 and 124. 
 
20. Fourth, the FTS had erred in failing to consider what remedies would be effective, just and 
appropriate by reference to section 8 of the 2024 Act. The respondent had duties under the 
2004 Act to make adequate and efficient provision for a child with additional needs, and 
was exercising a relevant function as defined in section 6 of the 2024 Act. If the respondent’s 
acts or failures to act were incompatible in connection with that function with the UNCRC 
requirements then 2024 conferred an entirely freestanding jurisdiction on the FTS to grant 
a remedy. Section 7 permitted a person to bring proceedings in any civil court or tribunal 
which had jurisdiction to grant the remedy sought.

21. When making final submissions in response to those of the respondent, Mr Nisbet drew to 
my attention the decision of the Inner House in JC v Gordonstoun Schools Limited 2016 SC 
758, an authority which he had recalled in the course of the hearing. He very candidly 
acknowledged that it might be read as reducing the force of some of his submissions 
regarding the duty on the tribunal to consider making orders not sought by the appellant. 
 
The respondent’s arguments 
 
22. The 2024 Act did not alter the jurisdiction of the FTS or confer any additional jurisdiction 
on it. The powers of the FTS in the present case were those conferred by part 3 of Schedule 
17 to the 2010 Act. The power under paragraph 9(2) of schedule 17 to make such order as 
the tribunal saw fit was qualified by the terms of paragraph 9(3) (a). Any order must be 
capable of obviating or reducing the adverse effect on the person of any matter to which 
the claim relates. Where an order ad factum praestandum was made, it must specify what 
was to be done and leave the respondent in no doubt as to the obligation that it must 
perform. It must be capable of being complied with. 
 
23. The words in the claim form, “ Also for the Education department to see and understand 
what impact this has had on [the child]” did not disclose that the appellant was seeking a 
competent remedy. The only remedy sought was reinstatement. The FTS did not require to 
consider what other remedies might be open to the appellant. Although the FTS might 
require, in compliance with rule 2(2)(c) of the 2017 Rules, to assist a party in the 
presentation of her case, without advocating the course he or she should take, the 
proceedings remained adversarial. 
 
24. It was far from clear, even by the time of the appeal, what the nature of the alleged 
discrimination was. Mr Anderson submitted that the first indication that it lay in a failure 
to make reasonable adjustments under section 20(3) came in Mr Nisbet’s oral submissions. 
The respondent’s written submission had proceeded on the assumption that the appellant’s 
case must be under section 15. 
 
25. The respondent had made representations to the FTS that the claim was not specified, and 
the legal basis for it was not clear , but the FTS had not required the appellant to provide 
further specification. It could and should have exercised its case management powers to 
obtain greater specification and to determine in due course whether there was any relevant 
claim before it.

26. None of the witnesses proposed by the appellant was in a position to give evidence in 
relation to the closure of the SA. The provision in rule 79(6) as to the entitlement of parties 
to call witnesses was obviously subject to the powers of the tribunal to exclude irrelevant 
evidence. 
 
27. There was no basis on which the FTS could have granted a declarator, assuming it had the 
power to make such an order. In any event, the appellant did not seek such an order. 
 
Decision 
 
28. It is unnecessary for the disposal of this appeal to express a concluded view about all of the 
arguments advanced by the parties about the jurisdiction of the FTS , the proper 
construction of paragraph 9 of schedule 17 to the 2010 Act, and the nature and extent of the 
remedies that the FTS may grant under those provisions if satisfied that there has been a 
contravention of chapter 1 of Part 6 of the 2010 Act. 
 
29. By the time that the FTS came to its decision, the appellant had clearly told the tribunal that 
the only remedy she wanted was the reinstatement of the child in the SA. Against that 
background, the argument that the terms of her claim form might have b een read as 
including a request for an apology from the respondent falls away. Where the FTS had 
formed the view that it would be inappropriate to grant the only remedy that the appellant 
was seeking, it would not have been in accordance with the principles set out in rule 2(2)(a) 
or (d) for it to have gone on to hear further evidence with a view to finding whether 
discrimination had occurred. Although the procedure adopted was unusual, the FTS did 
not err in law, in the particular circumstances of this case, by declining to consider whether 
unlawful discrimination had occurred. 
 
30. A tribunal is under no duty to construct a case that a party has not put before it. It follows, 
a fortiori (even more strongly) that it is under no duty to consider whether to grant a remedy 
that the party has not sought where she has clearly stated that she is interested only in 
obtaining one particular remedy. 
 
31. JC is a decision of the Inner House on an appeal from the Additional Suppor t Needs 
Tribunal for Scotland (ASNTS) in relation to a claim under the 2010 Act. The functions of 
the ASNTS were transferred to the FTS in terms of the First -tier Tribunal for Scotland 
(Transfer of Functions of the Additional Support Needs Tribunals for Scotland) Regulations

2018. At the time of the decision in JC, the procedural rules of the ASNTS were contained 
in the Additional Support Needs Tribunals for Scotland (Disability Claims Procedure) 
Rules SSI 2011/104. So far as claims under the 2010 Act are concerned, the rules are now 
in part 3 of the 2018 rules. The provisions of the 2011 rules regarding the overriding 
objective and the conduct of hearings (rules 3 and 29 respectively) do not differ in any 
material respect from those in rules 2 and 85 of the 2018 rules. The ratio of JC is binding 
on the FTS and on this Tribunal. 
 
32. In JC a child was excluded from a boarding school after having been found having sexual 
relations with another student on a teacher’s desk. The child had ADHD, and her mother 
brought a claim to the ASNTS. The tribunal was not satisfied that the child was disabled. 
They were not satisfied that the child’s mental impairment had a substantial and long term 
adverse effect on her ability to carry out normal day-to- day activities. They recognised 
that they required to consider her position without taking into account the beneficial effects 
of any medication. They were unable to make any relevant findings about that matter. 
There was evidence about the evidence the child was taking, but none about the effects on 
her if she had not taken that medication. Although they were not satisfied that the child 
was disabled, they went on to find that they were not satisfied that her actions rose in 
consequence of her ADHD. 
 
33. On appeal to the Court of Session, the mother maintained that the tribunal had erred in 
failing to find that the child’s executive functioning was impaired. They had failed to 
making findings in fact about the effect on the child of medical treatment, despite there 
being evidence about it. The tribunal ought to have explored the issue themselves. The 
school’s submission was that the mother had failed to lead evidence about the effect of 
medication, and that it was not for the tribunal to adopt an inquisi torial role. The court 
refused the appeal. Lady Smith said, at paragraph 55: 
 
“It is not the law that every person with a mental impairment is disabled for the purposes 
of the 2010 Act. That is only the case if it is established that the impairment in question is 
at a level which amounts to a substantial and long term adverse effect on normal day -to-
day activities. The onus of doing so lies firmly on the person seeking to advance a claim 
that there has been a contravention of a part of the Act. The role of the tribunal is not an 
inquisitorial one; whilst one of the observations by Morison J in Goodwin was to contrary 
effect, that was under reference to rules that used to, but are not now, applicable to 
Employment Tribunals, and subsequent decisions of the Employment Appeal Tribunal

have, in any event, corrected that impression. The onus is on the person claiming and the 
tribunal is not obliged to make its own enquiries: Joseph v Brighton & Sussex University 
Hospitals NHS Trust; Muschett v HM Prison Service; Rugamer v Sony Music Entertainment UK 
Ltd; Edinburgh Pharmaceutical Processes Ltd & Dr Newlands v Dr A P Lothian , para 107. We, 
accordingly, reject the suggestion that this tribunal was obliged to do so. The function of 
ASNTS was to hear the case that parties chose to put before it, make findings in fact and to 
decide the case in accordance with the relevant law. It was not part of its function to inquire 
into any case which the claimant might have but did not lead evidence about or advance in 
submission.” 
 
At paragraph 61, referring to the absence of evidence about the effects of medical treatment, 
Lady Smith wrote: 
 
“… no such evidence was led and it was not for the tribunal to go looking for it within that 
which was led to see if such a case could somehow be constructed or inferred; that was, 
essentially, the approach of senior counsel for the appellant. Nor, we would add, was it for 
the tribunal to seek to explore the issue with witnesses for themselves, particularly given 
that the appellant was legally represented. For the reasons to which we have already 
referred, if the appellant had a case to make about the effect of medical treatment, it was 
for her to make it. She did not do so.” 
 
It is clear that it is not for the tribunal to seek to construct a case where a party does not 
make that case before it. It is not obliged to consider remedies not sought by a claimant. 
Nothing in the reasoning of the Inner House would, however, necessarily preclude a 
tribunal from considering whether to grant a remedy other than that sought by a claimant, 
subject to the need to act in a procedurally fair manner. It is also fair to note that the Inner 
House made reference to the fact that the appellant was legally represented. I discuss below 
some of the tribunal’s case management powers. It may be particularly important, where 
a claimant is not represented, that those powers are exercised in such a way as to try to 
clarify the nature of her claim in fairness both to her and to the respondent. 
 
34. It is, therefore, unnecessary to reach a concluded view on the arguments of the parties 
about what other remedies the FTS might have granted had it found that there had been 
unlawful discrimination against the child. I note in passing that that the remedies sought 
in JC were a statement that the school discriminated against the pupil, a written apology to 
the pupil and her family, and training of school staff and alterations to the school’s

discipline policy to ensure that no similar incident occurred in the future. Although the 
issues in the appeal did not concern the remedies sought, there does not appear to have 
been any adverse comment from the court about the nature of those remedies, or 
suggestion that it would not have been competent for the tribunal to make the orders 
sought. 
 
35. I record that there was no merit in the submission that the witnesses for the claimant might 
have been relevant to the appropriateness of the remedy sought by the appellant. The FTS 
considered that matter, and was entitled to take the view that their evidence would not 
have been relevant to contradicting the evidence of A about the cessation of the service. 
The witnesses were Ms S, a family friend; and Ms C, the child’s grandmother. There was 
also a communication from the Child and Adolescent Mental Health Service. While the 
potential witnesses generally supported the view that the child should be readmitted to the 
SA because he had benefited from education there, they were not in a position to contradict 
A’s evidence about the cessation of the service at the SA. The FTS was entitled to find that 
it would not be appropriate to grant the remedy of reinstatement. 
 
36. I note also that there is nothing in the claimant’s bundle that obviously provides material 
that would have permitted the tribunal to address the prior question of whether the 
respondent had discriminated against the child, or (if the tribunal had any jurisdiction in 
the matter) whether the respondent had acted in a manner incompatible with the UNCRC 
requirements. 
 
37. A claim under section 15 of the 2010 Act would have required the tribunal to address 
whether the respondent had treated the child unfavourably because of something arising 
in consequence of his disability, and whether any such unfavourable treatment was a 
proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim. It not obvious from any material 
lodged by the appellant that cessation of the service at the SA was unfavourable treatment 
or that it arose in consequence of the child’s disability. 
 
38. A claim under section 19 of the 2010 Act would have required the tribunal to identify a 
provision, criteria or practice (PCP) which was discriminatory in relation to the child’s 
disability. It would have required to address the question of whether it was discriminatory 
having regard to the tests in section 19(2) of the 2010 Act. A case, such as that mentioned 
by Mr Nisbet in oral submissions, under sections 20(3) and 21, would again have required 
consideration of whether there was a PCP , and whether it put a disabled person at a

substantial disadvantage in relation to a relevant matter in comparison with persons who 
were not disabled. It would have required consideration of what steps were reasonable to 
avoid such a disadvantage, and whether there had been a failure to take such steps. 
 
39. On the facts of this case, no issue arises about a failure to consider a “freestanding UNCRC 
claim”. The part of the claim form said to have raised an issue simply referred to section 
6 of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child (Incorporation) (Scotland) 
2024 and quoted the terms of Article 28 of the UNCRC. On the hypothesis – which was 
disputed before me – that the FTS has jurisdiction in respect of a “freestanding UNCRC 
claim”, the appellant’s claim did not attempt to articulate why the conduct of the 
respondent in relation to any relevant function (as defined in section 6 of the 2024 Act) was 
unlawful because of any incompatibility with Article 28 of the UNCRC. 
 
40. Since I heard submissions, this tribunal has issued a decision in City of Edinburgh Council v 
SP 2026UT34 in relation to the jurisdiction of the FTS to consider “a freestanding UNCRC 
claim”. 
 
Observations regarding the tribunal’s case management powers 
 
41. By the time that a claim reaches a hearing, the role of the tribunal will generally be to listen 
to the evidence that the parties lead, and to the submissions of parties, and determine how 
to dispose of the claim. In a case under the 2010 Act, that will involve determining a 
number of mixed questions of fact and law relevant to one or more provisions of the 2010 
Act regarding discrimination. 
 
42. The 2018 rules provide opportunities for case management. If the claim does not state 
grounds of claim which a legal member considers sufficient to enable the responsible body 
to respond to it, the legal member must direct the claimant to send further and better 
particulars to the tribunal within a specified period. Where such a direction is made, the 
case statement period does not start to run until the direction has been complied with: rule 
63. If a party does not comply with such a direction the claim may be dismissed: rule 73. 
There is a power to dismiss on a range of other grounds, including the ground that the 
claim is frivolous or vexatious, in terms of rule 74. 
 
43. No order for further and better particulars was made in this case. Instead, the respondent 
was left to speculate as to whether the claim was one of direct discrimination or indirect

discrimination. All that the claim narrated was that a placement that worked for the child, 
and which the appellant thought was permanent, had been terminated. 
 
44. A case management hearing took place on 9 May 2025. The note of the call records: 
 
“The claimant confirmed that she does not wish to seek representation and is content to 
present her claim on her own. I explained that this is permissible and that rules exist that 
require the Tribunal to assist an unrepresented party to present their case, but not to give 
advice or suggest what course of action the party should take. On a related point, [the 
respondent’s solicitor] accepted that a broad approach should be taken to the legal 
arguments under the Equality Act 2010, given that the claimant is unrepresented. This is 
a perfectly reasonable approach, given the Tribunal rules.” 
 
Even if the solicitor acquiesced in a “broad approach” the tribunal should not have done 
so. It is not entirely clear what is meant by a “broad approach”, but the consequence of 
that approach was that the basis of the claim remained entirely unspecified. That was of 
assistance to no-one, including the appellant. That is illustrated by another passage in the 
note: 
 
“On witness statements content, again for the benefit of the claimant, these should be an 
account of facts relevant to and any views the witnesses have on the issues on the claim.” 
In the absence of clarification as to what those issues might be, the advice is likely to have 
been of little real use to the appellant. The only legal issue on which any direction was 
given was the competence of the remedy sought (presumably reinstatem ent). The 
respondent was to provide a submission in writing. At a minimum, the tribunal, the 
appellant and the respondent should all have known before the hearing started which 
provision or provisions of the 2010 Act the appellant was relying on . Clarification of that 
sort might have been the logical precursor of directions on issues on which evidence was 
required: rule 71(f)(i). 
45. There followed a further case management call on 21 August 2025. The note records: 
 
“[A different named solicitor for the respondent] agreed that a relaxed view would be taken 
of the usual requirement on the claimant to specify the type of discrimination that applies, 
given that the claimant is not leggaly [sic] represented. I suggested to the claimant that 
she might wish to read the Technical Guidance for Schools in Scotland issued by the EHRC,

available online, to help her understand some of the discrimination concepts that apply to 
the provision of education, again this is required under rule 2.” 
 
Mr Anderson told me that the solicitor disputed that she had in fact accepted that a “relaxed 
view” should be taken. Her position was that the note reflected the view of the tribunal, 
rather than her submission. I am not in a position to resolve that dispu te. That does not 
matter. Again, the tribunal should not have taken a “relaxed approach”. It is not 
compatible with the quality of case analysis that is necessary for the determination of a 
claim of this sort. It does not enable either party to focus on the evidence and legal 
submissions that will be necessary either to make good or to defend a claim of a particular 
type. 
 
46. It is in my view at least arguable that the tribunal stepped outwith the bounds of its 
statutory function when it directed the respondent to prepare and intimate a document 
setting out its proposed plan for the child’s “immediate future education”. I have no doubt 
that they did so with a view to trying to assist the appellant in her attempts to promote 
what she thought would be in the interests of the child. It is difficult, however, to see how 
the order that the tribunal made requiring an education plan sits within its jurisdiction, 
which is to determine the discrimination claim made to it under the 2010 Act. If the content 
of the education plan, looking to the future, had suggested discrimination against the child 
which might give rise to a remedy, then it would have been a new claim, on a new basis. 
The role of the tribunal is not to carry out a general inquiry into the child’s education, but 
to exercise its jurisdiction under the 2010 Act. 
 
A party to this case who is aggrieved by this decision may seek permission to appeal to the Court of Session 
on a point of law only. A party who wishes to appeal must seek permission to do so from the Upper Tribunal 
within 30 days of the date on which this decision was sent to him or her. Any such request for permission 
must be in writing and must (a) identify the decision of the Upper Tribunal to which it relates, (b) identify 
the alleged error or errors of law in the decision and (c) state in terms of sec tion 50(4) of the Tribunals 
(Scotland) Act 2014 what important point of principle or practice would be raised or what other compelling 
reason there is for allowing a further appeal to proceed. 
 
 
Lady Carmichael 
Member of the Upper Tribunal for Scotland
